title: Governance, Compliance and Medical Device Security

crumbs.name: Knowledge Based Professions and their Future

children.name: The AI Enablement Audit in Healthcare
children.blurb: An AI enablement audit in healthcare examines whether a clinical or operational setting can safely adopt, run, and oversee artificial intelligence systems.

children.name: Local Models for Patient Data
children.blurb: Local models for patient data are machine learning systems that process protected health information on hardware controlled by a healthcare organization, rather than sending it to a third-party cloud.

children.name: Software as a Medical Device
children.blurb: Software as a Medical Device covers software intended for medical purposes without being part of a physical device.

children.name: Bias in Clinical Triage
children.blurb: Bias in clinical triage covers systematic differences in how automated systems rank urgency, assign acuity scores, or allocate scarce resources such as beds, imaging, or specialist review.

children.name: Security of Connected Medical Devices
children.blurb: Security of connected medical devices covers the protection of networked clinical hardware such as infusion pumps, patient monitors, imaging systems, and implantable devices, along with their supporting software, data flows, and cloud or hospital interfaces.

sections.body: This section covers the practical work of governing AI in medicine, not the theory. Hospitals now run enablement audits before letting a model touch patient care, checking data access, model version, and fallback procedures. Local models are being deployed so that patient data stays inside a hospital's own servers instead of going to a cloud service. Regulators clear some software as a medical device, and researchers measure whether triage algorithms treat different patient groups differently. Security teams also monitor connected devices like infusion pumps and imaging machines for signs of tampering.
sections.heading: What this covers

sections.body: The field is uneven. This site tracks 1000 medical AI models and 803 scientific models, but a model existing in a paper or a product catalog is not the same as a model cleared for clinical use. Six active product liability and wrongful death lawsuits against AI companies show that legal responsibility is still being worked out. Audits are common but not standardized, so two hospitals can run very different checks. Local models reduce one kind of data exposure but do not solve access control or insider risk. Bias measurement in triage is improving, yet there is no agreed threshold for when a model is too biased to use. Connected device security remains a patchwork of old and new equipment, with many devices shipped without basic update mechanisms.
sections.heading: Where the work stands

sections.body: A reader should start with The AI Enablement Audit in Healthcare, which describes the pre-deployment review that ties the other pages together. Local Models for Patient Data explains one technical control for keeping patient records on site, and it pairs naturally with Security of Connected Medical Devices, which covers the hardware and network risks around those records. Software as a Medical Device is the regulatory page, showing what clearance means and what it does not cover. Bias in Clinical Triage is the clinical safety page, where fairness problems in urgent care algorithms are measured and documented. Together these pages move from the audit, to the technical and regulatory controls, to the specific harm of biased triage.
